article_text:
“ Obsession ” breakout Inde Navarrette appeared on “The Kyle Buchanan Show” and offered up her advice to Hollywood on how to keep Gen Z audiences interested in going to movie theaters. It’s not just about original storytelling, Navarrette argued, but also assuring young moviegoers that corporate slop won’t be force fed to them on the big screen.

“Gen Z just wants to go to something that they don’t feel like they’re being sold,” Navarrette said. “Maybe we are tired constantly of having ads in movies or production placement and all of these things. We understand it’s fundamental. We grew up with commercials that are fun that we still quote like State Farm and Aflac. It’s kind of fun. But we don’t want to be sold. We want original stories.”

“Just because we’re living in the time of technology doesn’t mean we’re not living a human life or feel human experiences,” she added. “I’m happy ‘Obsession’ brought that to the table. We want originality and we want to feel.”

“Obsession” turned Navarrette and co-star Michael Johnston into overnight sensations when it dominated the box office this summer on its way to a staggering $522 million global haul. Produced for less than $1 million, the Focus Features-released horror movie is one of the most profitable films in Hollywood history. Even more shocking was how “Obsession” kept earning more money at the box office for four consecutive weekends, becoming a Gen Z word of mouth blockbuster.

Perhaps Hollywood should listen to Navarrette. Variety reported on a Fandango study earlier this year that declared Gen Z the most active moviegoing demographic. The study found that 87% of Gen Zers and 82% of millennials saw at least one movie theatrically over the course of a year, compared to 70% of Gen Xers and 58% of baby boomers. Gen Z and millennials also returned more frequently, with each demo averaging about seven visits per year, ahead of Gen X (6.1) and baby boomers (5.7). The study noted Gen Z also spends more per visit on concessions and on premium format screens like Imax.

“While there has been a perception that Gen Z is less engaged with theatrical moviegoing, our data shows that their momentum has been building,” Fandango executive VP Jerramy Hainline said at the time. “What’s especially notable is how strongly they value the shared, communal aspect of the experience, reinforcing that theaters continue to play an important role as a social destination for younger audiences.”

article_text:
荏原 畠山美術館（東京・白金台）で10月17日（土）から12月13日（日）まで2026年秋季展が開催されます。 秋季展は「《畠山コレクション展》 異国へのあこがれ ―唐物、島物、古渡り」（本館2階）と「スタンランと猫のジャポニスム ―マネからシャ・ノワール（黒猫）、アール・ヌーヴォーの時代へ」（新館2階・地下1階）の2本立て。唐物や島物、古渡りなど茶道具の名品が集結するコレクション展と、ジャポニスムの魅力を体感できる展覧会という、二つの企画を同時に楽しむことができます。

《畠山コレクション展》 異国へのあこがれ ―唐物、島物、古渡り スタンランと猫のジャポニスム ―マネからシャ・ノワール（黒猫）、アール・ヌーヴォーの時代へ

会場：荏原 畠山美術館（東京都港区白金台2-20-12）

会期：2026年10月17日（土）～12月13日（日）

開館時間：10:00～17:00（入館は閉館の30分前まで）

休館日：月曜日（祝日の場合は開館、翌日休館）、11月17日（火）、11月18日（水）

観覧料：一般：1,500円／学生（高校生以上）： 1,000円 ※オンラインチケット割引有 中学生以下：無料（保護者同伴が必要）

アクセス：都営浅草線「高輪台」駅（A2出口）から徒歩5分／東京メトロ南北線・都営三田線「白金台」駅（1番出口）から徒歩10分

詳細は、 荏原 畠山美術館公式サイト まで。

異国へのあこがれ（本館2階）

茶の湯は、誕生の瞬間から常に「海の外にあるまだ見ぬ異国へのあこがれ」を原動力として発展してきました。その「あこがれ」は時代ごとに「賞揚（権威）」から「見立て（美学）」、そして「地球規模の交易」へと形を変えていきました。 本展では、最高峰の唐物や島物、古渡りの名品が集結します。かつての人々が異国の美に捧げた情熱と審美眼に触れられる貴重な機会です。時代を超えて私たちの心を捉えて離さない「異国へのあこがれ」の物語を、秋深まる美術館で堪能してみませんか。

スタンランと猫のジャポニスム（新館2階・地下1階）

19世紀末、浮世絵をはじめとする日本美術がパリで注目を集めると、西洋では長らく異端とされてきた猫が、モダン・アートを彩る重要なモチーフへと変貌しました。なかでも、猫を繰り返し描いた画家として知られるのが、フランス・パリで活躍したテオフィル=アレクサンドル・スタンランです。 本展ではスタンランを中心に、西洋の版画やポスター、日本の浮世絵など約100点を展示。さらに、初公開となるジャポニスム関連資料も紹介されます。猫という身近で魅力的な存在を入口に、19世紀末のパリで花開いた日本美術との出会いと、そこから生まれた新たな表現の世界を楽しむことができます。

公益財団法人 荏原 畠山記念文化財団が長年にわたりジャポニスム研究・交流を支えてきたことを背景に開催される展覧会です。

テオフィル=アレクサンドル・スタンラン（1859-1923年） 1859年11月10日、スイスのローザンヌに生まれる。はじめフランス東部のミュルーズで綿織物工場の図案家として働いた。1881年、妻エミリエとパリへ移り、以後モンマルトルを拠点に、挿絵、ポスター、版画、彫刻を制作。同年、ロドルフ・サリ（1851-1897）が開店したキャバレー「シャ・ノワール」で活動した。1890年代には、日本を題材としたバレエ「夢」のポスター（1890）、ボディニエール画廊での初個展（1894）、代表作≪シャ・ノワールの巡業≫（1896）などを手がけ、活躍の場を広げた。愛らしい猫を描きながら、擬人化を通して社会や人々の気質を風刺した。1923年12月14日パリのコランクール通り73番地で逝去。享年64。

（読売新聞美術展ナビ編集班）

article_text:
The Austin Film Festival has announced the winners of its script and film competition. The 33rd annual event received more than 12,500 submissions, with 78 scripts advancing to the finalist round before the festival selected 21 writers and writing teams as winners. Those honored received their awards during the Awards Luncheon on Saturday in Austin, Texas.

“For more than 30 years, our competitions have been about recognizing great scriptwriting,” Barbara Morgan, Executive Director of Austin Film Festival, said. “We want talented storytellers to leave Austin with more than an award. We want them to leave with new relationships, meaningful industry access and opportunities that can help move their careers forward. This year’s winners represent exactly the kind of bold, original voices we are proud to champion.”

Related Stories

'Glee' Reboot Officially Set at Disney+ and Hulu

Katseye's New Documentary 'Wild Hearts' Is Officially Streaming on Hulu

These awards aim to help emerging talent be discovered by agents, managers, producers, executives and other industry leaders seeking new voices. AFF connects competition finalists with industry professionals through its Writers Conference and Producers Book, which features finalist projects and contact information for writers. Many awards include tailored fellowship opportunities designed to provide mentorship, industry access and career development. Winners in the narrative, documentary and animated shorts competitions are also eligible for Academy Award consideration.

A panel of showrunners, creators, producers, and writers with credits including “Widows Bay,” “The Bear,” “Succession,” “Parks and Rec,” and more selected the winning projects. See the full list of winners below.

Scripted Digital Series Award — “Old Bogus Massacre” by Matthew McFadden, Dawn Cowle and Baylor Knobloch

2026 Film Competition Award & Fellowship Winners

Animated Short — “How Not to Die on an Alien Planet” Writer: Carlos F. Puertolas, Anthony Hodgson; Director: Carlos F. Puertolas

Produced Digital Series — “Matched” Writer: Dominique Salerno, Director: Elvira Ibragimova

Private visits to the Paris studio of Louis Stettner are open again during Paris Photo week for a fifth year. From November 9 to 14, collectors are invited to spend an hour inside the studio, with appointments available between 10am and 6pm each day, Paris time.

Each visit is one hour and limited to a single party of up to ten guests, so you can take your time. You will see original prints, contact sheets and personal materials from a career that moved between Paris and New York, with the Estate of Louis Stettner there to welcome you.

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "朴栖甫（Park Seo-Bo，1931–2023）是一位韩国艺术家。他于 2019 年创立了 GIZI 基金会，后来更名为 PARKSEOBO FOUNDATION。该基金会负责管理朴栖甫的艺术作品与档案、组织展览，并于 2026 年 8 月在首尔开设了 PARKSEOBO MUSEUM（朴栖甫美术馆），举办了开幕展《朴栖甫与香道：空满之间》（Park Seo-Bo & Huong Dodinh: Emptiness Fullness），将这位韩国艺术家的作品与一位越南裔法国女画家（其创作独立发展）的作品进行了跨时空的对话。朴承浩是艺术家的儿子，现任该基金会理事长。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ArtReview 基金会是以您已故的父亲命名的。他在基金会的筹建过程中参与了多少？其宗旨又是什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "朴承浩 基金会于 2019 年在朴栖甫的倡议下成立。当时我父亲即将步入九旬，他觉得需要有一种方式来传承他已经取得的成就以及尚未能实现的目标。他一生致力于艺术创作，同时也不断为韩国艺术的发展做出贡献。我相信他强烈地感受到，必须有一个坚实的基金会，才能确保这些努力在未来不会消逝。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们最重要的职责之一就是管理、保护和传播朴栖甫的遗产。他经历了韩国历史上动荡巨变的一时期。他一直试图站在变革的前沿，在艺术界发出强有力的声音。正因如此，他的档案中蕴含着远超单一艺术家历史的宏大故事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们也希望基金会能成为一个能够对下一代艺术家产生积极影响的机构。这与 2026 年 8 月开馆的美术馆的使命紧密相连。朴栖甫认为，与同代人共同发展，比独自成为一个享誉全球的人物更有意义、更有力量。正因如此，他悉心培养年轻艺术家，支持后来者。我们希望基金会能继续履行这一角色。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Sam_Profile-1230x1845.png", "alt": "PARKSEOBO FOUNDATION 理事长朴承浩", "caption": "PARKSEOBO FOUNDATION 理事长朴承浩", "credit": "ArtReview", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "AR 您提到基金会有两个角色：一个是照顾朴栖甫的遗产、他的作品以及作品的呈现方式；另一个是支持新一代艺术家，他们的理念可能与朴栖甫有着根本的不同。您是如何平衡这两者的？它们之间是否曾有过冲突？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "SP 我不认为传承朴栖甫的遗产仅仅意味着保存他留下的作品。朴栖甫不仅是一位画家，还是一位行动主义者和管理者。在 20th 世纪 1960 年代，韩国刚从长期的战争创伤中走出，国内艺术界百废待兴，他协助创立了韩国美术协会等组织，并鼓励身边的艺术家继续他们的艺术实践。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他还竭尽所能让韩国艺术家参与双年展，并不懈地将韩国艺术介绍给世界。为了发掘新锐艺术家，他创立了一个名为《Indépendants》的展览系列。他还组织了“首尔群展”（École de Séoul），为韩国艺术的发展做出了贡献。在他的一生中，他始终认为大都市以外地区的艺术发展同样重要。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": Park Seo-Bo (1931–2023) was a Korean artist. He founded the GIZI Foundation in 2019, later renamed the PARKSEOBO FOUNDATION. The foundation manages Park’s artworks and archives, organises exhibitions and in August 2026 opened the PARKSEOBO MUSEUM, in Seoul, with the exhibition Park Seo-Bo & Huong Dodinh: Emptiness Fullness , which posthumously puts the Korean artist’s work in dialogue with that of the Vietnamese-born French painter, whose work developed independently. Sam Seungho Park, the artist’s son, is the chairperson of the foundation.

ArtReview The foundation is named after your late father. To what extent was he involved in setting it up and what are its aims?

Sam Seungho Park The foundation was established in 2019, at Park Seo-Bo’s initiative. As my father was approaching the age of ninety, he felt that there needed to be a way to carry forward both what he had accomplished and what he had not yet been able to achieve. He had devoted his entire life to working as an artist while also making continuous efforts to contribute to the development of Korean art. I believe he strongly felt that a solid foundation was necessary to ensure that these efforts would not disappear in the future.

One of our foremost responsibilities is to manage, preserve and communicate Park Seo-Bo’s legacy. He lived through a period of tremendous upheaval in the history of the Republic of Korea. He consistently sought to be at the forefront of change and to speak with a strong voice in the artworld. For that reason, his records contain a much broader story than simply the history of one artist.

We also hope that the foundation will become an institution capable of having a positive influence on artists of the next generation. This is closely connected to the mission of the museum that opened in August 2026. Park Seo-Bo believed that it was more meaningful and powerful to develop together with his peers than to become a globally recognised figure on his own. That is why he nurtured younger artists and supported those who came after him. We hope that the foundation will continue to fulfil this role.

AR You mentioned the foundation has two roles: one is caring for Park Seo-Bo’s legacy, his work and how it is presented; the other is supporting new generations of artists, who might have radically different ideas from those that Park Seo-Bo had. How do you manage the two? Do they ever come into conflict?

SP I don’t believe that carrying forward Park Seo-Bo’s legacy means simply preserving the works he left behind. Park Seo-Bo was not only a painter, but also an activist and an administrator. In the 1960s, after Korea had emerged from the long aftermath of war and little remained of the country’s artworld, he helped establish organisations such as the Korean Fine Arts Association, and he encouraged the artists around him so that they could continue their artistic practices.

He also made every possible effort to enable Korean artists to participate in biennales and consistently worked to introduce Korean art to the world. To discover emerging artists, he created an exhibition series called Indépendants . He also organised École de Séoul in order to contribute to the development of Korean art. Throughout his life, he believed that artistic development in the regions beyond the metropolitan area was also important.

In this sense, the foundation’s vision of preserving Park Seo-Bo’s legacy while becoming a platform for a new generation is not that different from the role he himself played throughout his life. As for whether new artists need to share Park Seo-Bo’s aesthetic sensibilities, there was a motto displayed in the classroom where Park Seo-Bo concluded his career as an educator. It read, ‘Do not resemble your friends, do not feel indebted to history, and do not resemble your teacher.’

At a time when authoritarianism was widespread in Korea, and perhaps across the wider world, this was a radical message. Yet until the very end of his life, Park Seo-Bo urged artists to remain wholly creative. We still need to do that, and this is what the foundation would also like to encourage.

AR The foundation runs a programme that makes the canvases Park Seo-Bo prepared but didn’t use during his lifetime available for new artists to work with. Was that his idea, or an idea that came afterwards?

SP It was not Park Seo-Bo’s intention to repurpose his canvases; when he was alive, he wanted to continue working as an artist until he was one hundred. After he passed away, the foundation decided to use his canvases as an extension of his philosophy of encouraging younger artists. Had my father decided during his lifetime to stop working, I think he might well have shared his remaining canvases with younger artists in the same way.

AR How do you choose which younger artists to work with?

SP Although I’m in charge of this foundation, I’ve only been deeply interested in art for six years. I’ve studied extensively to understand what art is, and I visit a lot of graduate exhibitions and galleries to explore which artists are creating meaningful work and standing out. I also look through their personal websites, Instagram accounts and other channels to get a sense not only of their work but also of their attitude as artists. Through this process, we find young artists we can work with. When I discover a promising artist, I contact them directly, purchase their work and provide them with canvases, and ask them to create new works.

AR What is the purpose of the new museum, and why do you need a physical space to further the aims of the foundation?

SP Compared with the history of Western art, the history of Korean contemporary art has been quite difficult. Korea’s period under Japanese colonial rule almost severed the continuity of traditional culture. This was followed by the Korean War, and it would not be an exaggeration to say that almost nothing was left at the time. For that reason, it is fair to say that Korean contemporary art has a history of only a little over seventy years. There are, therefore, aspects of Korea’s art ecosystem that still need to be developed. Park Seo-Bo’s decision to establish the foundation and donate all of his remaining artworks to it, so that people could have access to them, can be understood as part of a new development that is only just beginning in Korea.

On the other hand, through research into and exhibitions about his artistic world, we seek to shed new light on its meaning within a contemporary context. We hope to keep his art alive in the present and to continue an ongoing dialogue with the contemporary art scene. Rather than relying on authority and convention, Park Seo-Bo discovered new artists on the basis of their potential and talent, and opened pathways for them to encounter a wider world. We seek to carry forward this spirit by providing a foundation for creators to develop their abilities freely and advance onto the international stage. The physical space of a museum gives us an effective way to put these convictions into practice. A single action can be worth more than a hundred words.

AR Would the foundation ever sell any of Park Seo-Bo’s work in order to support its mission of helping younger artists?

SP Our goal is to manage the entire legacy, not only the paintings but also the other assets, so that the foundation and museum can continue to operate sustainably. The legacy consists of Park Seo-Bo’s artwork and financial resources. If you were to sell all of his work, there would be nothing left to exhibit in the museum, right? At the same time, operating a foundation and museum requires substantial financial resources. If it becomes difficult to maintain them, we may have to sell some of his works. Even then, we select buyers so that his works can be displayed in public art museums where many people can see them, rather than hanging in someone’s private living room. Let me reiterate that selling the paintings is not our fundamental management strategy. Our priority is to preserve his collection and ensure the long-term sustainable operation of the foundation and the museum.

AR What have some of the biggest challenges been in setting up the foundation and the museum?

SP It was not that difficult to establish a foundation, but the greater challenge was securing the resources needed to hire qualified professionals to archive his works and conduct the necessary research. In terms of establishing the museum, the main difficulty was, of course, financial. Land and construction costs in Seoul are high these days. We had to reduce the museum’s scale. That is one aspect of the project I regret in some ways.

AR How has your perspective on the art scene changed since you became involved in the foundation?

SP Before entering the art world, I had been a university professor. Although I had always been familiar with art through my father, I was not as knowledgeable about the field as I am today. But being chairman of the board of this foundation is, in a way, my destiny because of who my father was. To operate this foundation properly after his passing, I felt that I needed to understand the art scene: the art world, younger artists, the market, everything. In fact, I came to see dynamics in the art market that I could never have seen from the perspective of an ordinary viewer or an outsider to this world. I also began to examine the education system and government cultural policy. I think this was a learning process I needed to go through to do my best in this role.

AR How would you measure success for the foundation?

SP Now that the museum has been created, it feels as if we have been given an entirely new mission for the future. The roles of the foundation and the museum are somewhat different. Visitor numbers could be a good measure of the museum’s success, but not the foundation’s success, I think. The foundation’s work is assessed differently. First and foremost, we must compile a comprehensive body of scholarly research materials on Park Seo-Bo and carry out that work to the highest standard. Since those materials inevitably encompass his contemporaries, this is less an archive of Park Seo-Bo alone than an archive of Korean contemporary art. That makes the process all the more meaningful and important. At the same time, we can contribute to a broader cultural legacy by supporting exhibitions, research and documentation relating to the young artists the foundation supports. I think the foundation’s success can be judged by the results of these efforts.

AR How do you see the role of the foundation and museum developing or evolving in the future?

SP For young artists, I hope it will be a reliable source of support, a place they can turn to, and for mid-career artists, I hope it will become a model they can look to. For the general public, I hope it will be a welcoming space. I hope the foundation and the museum can become their playground in the future.

article_text:
Hollywood is a business of people. Yesterday, the industry got a reminder of that when Warner Bros. and DC Studios announced that Steven Soderbergh will help director Matt Reeves finish production on “The Batman Part II” while Reeves deals with a family matter.

“Just to be clear, I am not leaving ‘The Batman Part II,'” Reeves wrote on X shortly after the news broke. “I am profoundly grateful to Steven for coming to my aid during this challenging time to help me finish principal photography. Thank you to all for your concern and well wishes.”

This, of course, is not the first time in the history of popular cinema that an outside director stepped in to take a project over the finish line. However, few of the other switches were done with friendship, collaboration and support, as is the case with Soderbergh and Reeves. Whether it was ballooning budgets, off-camera scandal, or personal differences, Hollywood has no shortage of studios scrambling to replace their director when disaster struck.

Here is a list of seven instances in movie history where a film had to be finished by a second director.

Spartacus (1960) – Anthony Mann Replaced by Stanley Kubrick Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection Star Kirk Douglas, whose company, Bryna Films was producing “Spartacus,” was the one calling the shots on this classic gladiator movie, as far as the director was concerned. After two weeks of shooting, Douglas got the approval of the studio to replace Anthony Mann, an experienced director of Westerns, saying Mann had lost control and was letting co-star Peter Ustinov direct his own scenes. Douglas brought in Stanley Kubrick, who had directed him in “Paths of Glory,” and the film ended up winning four Oscars as well as the Golden Globe for best drama. “Spartacus” was Universal Pictures’ highest-grossing film until “Airport” 10 years later.

Bohemian Rhapsody (2018) – Bryan Singer Replaced by Dexter Fletcher Image Credit: 20th Century Fox/Moviestore/REX/ “Bohemian Rhapsody” was already several months into production when director Bryan Singer failed to return to set after the Thanksgiving break. The studio temporarily halted production due to a “health matter” involving Singer — his mother was later revealed to have been ill — but reports swirled about Singer’s unreliability on set, verbal abuse and his alleged disagreements with star Rami Malek. Dexter Fletcher, who was previously attached to the project, was brought in to replace Singer and finish the final third of the film. Though he wasn’t mentioned in promotional materials , Singer received a sole directorial credit, in line with DGA guidelines, and Fletcher was credited as executive producer. It became the highest-grossing musical biopic until “Michael” was released, and won four Oscars in addition to a best picture nomination.

Justice League (2017) – Zack Snyder Replaced by Joss Whedon Image Credit: ©Warner Bros/courtesy Everett Collection / Everett Collection “Justice League” is one of the most famous recent examples of a director swap. In 2017, Zack Snyder stepped away from the film during post-production to grieve with his family after his daughter took her own life. Joss Whedon, who five years earlier hit big directing Marvel’s “Avengers,” was brought in and made sweeping changes to the film. Allegations of misconduct followed, and the understandable outrage of Snyder fans eventually led to the 2021 release of “The Snyder Cut” of “Justice League,” which clocked in at just over four hours. During a recent sit-down with Variety , Snyder said he’s never seen Whedon’s version of “Justice League,” given the hardships he and his family were experiencing at the time of release: “I’ve never seen it. There was a point when the movie was released that was a low point for me because the pile-on effect was so insane. Not only did I lose my daughter, but also they’ve released this version of the movie that I had nothing to do with and my name is on a movie that I didn’t make.”

The Island of Dr. Moreau (1996) – Richard Stanley Replaced by John Frankenheimer Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection The production of “The Island of Dr. Moreau” was an absolutely legendary debacle. Original director Richard Stanley had been developing his pet project for four years when New Line recruited Marlon Brando to star as mad scientist Dr. Moreau. New Line wanted Roman Polanski to direct, but Brando appreciated Stanley’s vision and the film lurched into production in Australia. Bruce Willis had already dropped out of the film, with Val Kilmer stepping in and immediately acting erratically, while Brando’s daughter died by suicide before principal photography began. Two days into production, while a hurricane raged across the region, co-star Rob Morrow quit, and one day later Stanley was fired by New Line. Veteran director John Frankenheimer was brought in, though the tensions continued, with both Brando and Frankenheimer tangling with Kilmer. The film’s fired production staff later reported that Stanley returned to set in a dog-man costume and acted as an extra in the film he was fired from. The film flopped and swept the Razzie Awards nominations.

Superman II (1981) – Richard Donner Replaced by Richard Lester Image Credit: ©Warner Bros/Courtesy Everett Collection Father-and-son producer duo Alexander and Ilya Salkind made the bold choice in 1977 to film “Superman” and “Superman II” simultaneously, much to the chagrin of director Richard Donner. Tensions rose to such a boil that they decided to stop production on the sequel and focus on getting the first “Superman” in the can. “Superman II,” at that point, was mostly finished. After the first film dropped in 1978, Donner was pink-slipped and replaced by Richard Lester, who reshot most of “Superman II” so he could be credited as director. In 1978, famed Variety columnist Army Archerd caught up with producer Pierre Spengler at a Christmas party. The French producer told Archerd that despite tensions on the first “Superman,” he was looking forward to collaborating with Donner on the sequel. Archerd then followed up with Donner, who told him of shooting the sequel with Spengler, “If he’s on it, I’m not.”

Brave (2012) Brenda Chapman Replaced by Mark Andrews Image Credit: ©Walt Disney Co./Courtesy Everett Collection Brenda Chapman spent six years developing and writing the screenplay for “Brave,” which was based on her relationship with her daughter and featured Pixar’s first female protagonist. Chapman came on as Pixar’s first female director, only to be replaced by Mark Andrews due to “creative differences” with John Lasseter. “I think it’s a really sad state. We’re in the 21st century and there are so few stories geared towards girls, told from a female point of view,” Chapman told the L.A. Times. “Brave” ended up winning the Oscar for best animated feature, with Chapman and Andrews credited as co-directors.

Solo: A Star Wars Story (2018) – Phil Lord and Christopher Miller Replaced by Ron Howard Image Credit: ©Walt Disney Co./courtesy Everett / Everett Collection Phil Lord and Christopher Miller, the directors behind this year’s sci-fi box office smash “Project Hail Mary,” were originally set to direct “Solo: A Star Wars Story.” After a lengthy casting process, shooting began in January 2017, and by June 2017, Lord and Miller were out. Lucasfilm cited “creative differences” as the reason for the exit, and Ron Howard was brought in as a replacement with most of the movie already shot. It was later reported that Lucasfilm boss Kathleen Kennedy clashed with Lord and Miller over tonal issues and the loose shooting style they brought to what production considered an ironclad screenplay. Hanging over all this behind-the-scenes drama was an ever-increasing production budget, which topped out at around $275 million. The movie only made $392 million worldwide, marking a major bomb for Disney and Lucasfilm.

article_text:
Queer Gaze est la rubrique de notre journaliste Timé Zoppé sur le cinéma LGBTQ+.

Mon éducation à la queerness au travers des images de cinéma s’est beaucoup faite par des figures féminines. Parce que mon père aime une seule chose dans la vie : Almodovar ! Et la culture hispanique, parce qu’on est espagnol dans la famille. Il y avait aussi ces grandes figures féminines : Rossy de Palma, Carmen Maura et Victoria Abril, qui avait déjà quelque chose de Loli, son personnage dans Gazon maudit de Josiane Balasko (1996). J’ai compris plus tard qu’elles étaient des figures queer et ça m’a pas mal nourri.

Après, mon imaginaire queer s’est beaucoup développé sur la « non-image » dans le cinéma, je pense notamment au film Sexe Intentions (1999) de Roger Kumble que j’adorais quand j’étais jeune, où il y a un personnage gay qui est payé pour avoir une relation avec un mec hétéro. Rien n’est montré, mais la suggestion de cette homosexualité ou de cette bisexualité, ça me rendait fou ! Je pense aussi à Elephant (2003) de Gus Van Sant, quand les deux gamins qui s’apprêtent à faire la tuerie s’embrassent, comme deux ados complètement perdus qui s’apprêtent à faire quelque chose de fou et qui du coup se disent “Y a plus de tabou, y’a plus rien qui tient”.

A l’adolescence, avec les premiers réseaux sociaux, MySpace et tout, j’ai eu la chance de me retrouver dans les groupes de personnes qui allaient voir les films de Bruce LaBruce , John Waters , Gregg Araki … J’ai grandi à Toulouse, où il y avait pas mal de cinéma arty et indépendants, donc on avait quand même la possibilité de voir ces films-là. J’étais dans des petites communautés qui organisaient des espèces de mini-festivals où ces films passaient. Donc j’ai été beaucoup marqué par cette imagerie très pop, très queer, au-delà de gay, très colorée, très saturée, très engagée. Épileptique, quoi !

J’ai appris ce qu’était le cabaret en le faisant. Je suis directement arrivée chez Madame Arthur [le premier cabaret travesti de Paris, ouvert en 1946, ndlr] qui reste un lieu d’histoire queer primordial, un des premiers à avoir accueilli des personnes travesties sur scène et aussi et surtout des personnes trans. Pour moi, il y a cette idée qu’une fois qu’on s’est débarrassé de tous les tabous, et notamment du tabou ultime qui est celui du genre, ça ouvre un champ d’exploration artistique infini.

Parmi les films de cabaret qui m’ont marqué au cinéma, je pense à Moulin Rouge (2001) et Roméo + Juliette (1996) de Baz Luhrmann, tous ces films qui ont quelque chose de camp , de débonnaire. Tous les films que j’ai cités avant ont justement cet élément du cabaret qui est celui du camp, du kitsch, de l’outrance, des mondes un peu épileptiques dans lesquels il n’y a que du trop et pas de ridicule. J’aime beaucoup les films musicaux en général et j’ai beaucoup aimé Phantom of the Paradise (1974) de Brian de Palma, qui était vraiment mon film favori dans ma fin d’adolescence et que j’ai poncé. Le Rocky Horror Picture Show (1975) de Jim Sharman, évidemment ! C’est typiquement un film qu’on s’est passé sous le manteau avec les copains au lycée.

Je trouve qu’aujourd’hui les conditions de création du cinéma indépendant sont de plus en plus compliquées, et que c’est ahurissant et regrettable de voir que tous les films queer qui ont de la visibilité sont majoritairement signés par des mecs blancs cis. J’ai suivi de près avec un peu de tristesse ce qui s’est passé autour de Jim Queen (2026) [des spectateur-ices ont reproché au film un manque de diversité et des clichés homophobes, ndlr] de Nicolas Athané et Marco Nguyen, et pour moi c’est représentatif d’un monde où ces histoires ont du mal à se raconter. Quand un film queer important pour la communauté sort, je me bouge pour aller le voir. Et si j’y vais pas souvent, c’est peut-être aussi qu’il n’y en a pas assez !

Je suis en couple avec une femme trans et je n’ai rien à me mettre sous la dent en termes de représentation. À 37 ans, il y a plein de choses que j’aimerais comprendre grâce à des représentations au cinéma, et la dernière fois que j’ai vu un film qui montrait une histoire comme celle-là, c’était Laurence Anyways (2012) de Xavier Dolan – on parle d’un film qui a de l’âge. On ne voit pas assez de films réalisés par des personnes trans, par des femmes, notamment des films sur la queerness réalisés par des femmes.

Ce que j’aimerais aujourd’hui, c’est qu’il y ait un queer gaze au cinéma sur tout un tas de choses. J’adorerais voir un film sur l’architecture fait par une personne queer, avec ce regard-là, sans que ce soit le thème central. Je trouve que dans les archives de John Waters, Gregg Araki, on retrouve un queer gaze posé sur des choses qui ne parlent pas de ça.

article_text:
作曲家としても活動するアーティストの新作絵画を一挙展示

京都市京セラ美術館 で 「Liminal – 池内ヨシカツ展」 が10月25日まで開催されている。作曲家・美術家の池内ヨシカツの新作絵画を中心に音によるアート作品も併せて展示する個展。入場無料。

池内は京都市出身、東京在住。高校生の頃から自身の楽曲をインターネット上で発表して本格的に作曲活動を開始。エレクトロミュージックを軸に、坂本龍一が音楽を担当した映画『怒り』（2016）の劇中曲をはじめ、数多くの映画・CM音楽の作曲や有名ミュージシャンとのコラボ楽曲を手がけてきた。画家の祖父に技術を教わった絵画の制作にも取り組み、香港や韓国、タイなどアジア各地でグループ展やアートフェアに参加。日本国内でのアート個展は、昨年の 京都国立博物館 での開催に続き、本展が2回目となる。

池内は、作曲と絵画の双方に取り組む理由と本展について次のように話す。

「作曲家として言葉や映像を音楽に置き換える実践が増えるなかで、異なる表現間の隔たりやそのあいだに生じる『生まれるもの』『失われるもの』に関心を持ち、幼い頃から親しみ独学で学んできた絵画の制作を本格的に始めた。音楽と絵画はそれぞれ異なる時間と距離を持ち、そのあいだに生まれる関係は、両者が出合うたびにかたちを変えていく。本展では、来場者の方が音楽と絵画のあいだに関係を見いだし、関係を結び直す経験をしていただければと思う」

「見る行為の入り口」として描く子供のモチーフ

本展会場の京都市京セラ美術館本館「光の広間」は、かつて中庭だった場所を改修してガラスの大屋根を架け室内化したスペースだ。そのダイナミックな空間性を生かし、本展では中央に池内の絵画に基づく巨大バナーを掲げ、それを取り囲むように新作の油彩画23点と立体作品3点を展示。池内のサウンドインスタレーションや、作曲と絵画制作を行うスタジオを再現したコーナーも設置して、音楽と美術という異領域を自在に行き来する創作活動を伝える。

展示されている絵画は、すべて子供をモチーフとし、光を湛えた大きな目や簡略化した顔立ちといった漫画的な記号性と古典的な描法が画面に同居する。奇妙な生き物を抱いたりシャボン玉に頭部に覆われたりといった非現実的なシチュエーション、透明感がある柔らかい色彩も目を引く。

鑑賞者の見方により受け止め方が変わる、子供の表情や身体の表現が印象的だ。半身像の《A Trace of Seeing》は、身体の一部が背景に溶け込むモザイク状に置き換えられ、その姿は消失していくようにも出現しつつあるようにも見える。顔を大きく描いた《Elusive》の子供は、泣いているようだが、こちらを見つめる大きな瞳には幾つも小さな光が揺れ、説明できない複雑な感情を訴えているようにも映る。

「音楽と歴史的に関わりが深い抽象画ではなく、具象画を描くのは絵画を『見る行為の入り口』と自分はとらえているから。日常的なモチーフが徐々に見慣れないものに変わっていく。そんな認識と実体のズレを表現したいと考えたとき、いちばんしっくりきたテーマが子供だった」（池内）。

目に見えないが、本展のために池内が制作したサウンドインスタレーションも重要な要素。入り口上方の中2階から3つの異なる音が流れ、会場で立つ位置により聞こえ方が多様に変わるように仕組まれている。それぞれの音は異なる周期でリピートされるため、その重なり具合も変化し続け、「目の前にある絵画の印象の変化や一瞬の音との出会いを楽しんでもらえたら」と池内は話す。

絵画と音楽の「Liminal」（境界）にある「互換性の空隙」

現代美術を専門とする文化研究者の山本浩貴は、池内の絵画と音楽を、「密接に結びつきながら、互いに独立して存在しているもの」と位置付けたうえで、次のように話す。

「本展を『Liminal』（境界）と題したように、池内は絵画と音楽のあいだにある『互換性の空隙』、つまり翻訳不可能な部分を探求している。以前対談したとき、池内は左耳の難聴をきっかけに自分の呼吸や心拍といった身体音に意識が向いたと語っていた。外界の音から自身の内側で鳴る“生命の音”へと関心を拡張した経験が、人間の『見る』『聴く』行為を広くとらえ、その境界線に目を凝らす姿勢をうながしたように思える」

また山本は、池内の絵画に登場する子供の多くが男児とも女児とも見分けがたい点にも注目する。「日本のカワイイ文化や漫画・アニメ文化の文脈に連なる作品は、少女を性的対象として描くものが多く、それゆえに批判もされていた。だが池内が描く子供像は、そうしたサブカルチャーの影響を受けながらも、セクシュアリティやジェンダーを明確に示す有徴性は少ない。従来のサブカル的な価値観や表象を更新する新しい世代性を作品から感じる」と語る。

なお本展は、京都の新たな文化的価値の発信を目指し、府の企業版ふるさと納税を活用して若手アーティストを育成・支援する取り組み「NEW GENERATION ART PROJECT」として行われた。本プロジェクトは、来年1月にも池内の個展を京都市で予定しており、マルチな創作活動の展開に出合える機会は続く。

editorial_excerpt_zh: 跨越边界：这位波兰导演探讨了她的最新作品，这部电影直面在其祖国发生的难民危机

Border）——发现了一具因体温过低而死男子的尸体。“那个年轻人的形象，”霍兰在一次采访中说道，“在我的祖国这里冻死……实在是太可怕了。面对这场由政客制造的危机，作为艺术家、作为人类、作为社会、作为国家，我们必须表明鲜明的立场。”45年来，霍兰在反对法西斯主义和威权主义、反对父权制和对女性压迫的电影中，一直坚定地秉持道德、社会和政治立场。其中的杰作至少有两部——《欧洲欧洲》（1990年），一部狂热喜剧却又完全基于事实的大屠杀幸存故事；以及生态女性主义惊悚片《糜骨之壤》（2017年），这让人想起艾萨克·巴舍维斯·辛格（Isaac "霍兰的最新力作《绿边》具有小说的结构，分为四个紧密相连的章节和一个尾声。影片开场讲述了一个叙利亚家庭以及其他来自中东和非洲的难民试图从白俄罗斯越境，白俄罗斯总统曾公开承诺他们可以安全通往波兰，并从波兰前往欧盟的任何地方。然而这些承诺全无兑现，难民们在边境铁丝网上遭到边防卫兵的推搡和粗暴驱赶。有些人不幸身亡，但也有人设法逃入了波兰一侧的茂密森林和险恶沼泽中。随着剧情推进，影片的焦点转向了一名波兰边防卫兵，接着是一群因遵循政府规则而毫无用处的救援人员，最后是一位决定脱离维权人士、将三名来自刚果的年轻男子护送到安全屋的女性。", "边界上的那片森林——这些事情正是在那里发生的——是一片原始森林，属于国家。我们知道我们不可能在那里拍摄这样一部电影。我们不想让政府知道我们在做什么。事实上，那片森林离华沙太远了——我们没有来回奔波的差旅资金。但我们看过关于那片森林中所发生事情的纪录片报道，我们附近有一片森林，看起来与之足够相似。那是一个有限的空间，但足以重现真实发生的事情。森林真的很重要。它既需要逼真，又得带有一种恐怖故事里的森林感——对于那些以为自己会来到天堂却落入此境的难民来说，它会是怎样的。我们总共只用 article_text:
A few years ago, a friend of the Polish director Agnieszka Holland found the body of a man who had died of hypothermia in the exclusionary zone at the border between Poland and Belarus—the Green Border. “The image of that young man,” Holland said in an interview, “freezing to death here in my country . . . is so horrible. In the face of this crisis manufactured by politicians, we must take a clear position as artists, as people as a society, as a country.” For 45 years, Holland has been taking clear moral, social, and political positions in films that speak out against fascism and authoritarianism, against patriarchy and the oppression of women. Among them are at least two masterpieces— Europa Europa (1990), a wildly comic but completely factual Holocaust survival story; and the eco-feminist thriller Spoor (2017), which brings to mind a remark by Isaac Bashevis Singer: “In relation to [animals], all people are Nazis; for the animals, it is an eternal Treblinka.”

Green Border , Holland’s latest, is structured novelistically, with four interlocking chapters and an epilogue. The film opens with a Syrian family and other migrants from the Middle East and Africa attempting to cross the border from Belarus, whose president had made public promises of safe passage into Poland, from which they could travel anywhere in the European Union. None of this turns out to be true, and the migrants are literally pushed and tossed back and forth across barbed-wire fencing by border guards. Some die, but some manage to escape into the deep forest and treacherous swamps on the Polish side. As the film continues, its focus shifts to a Polish border guard, then to a group of aid workers who play by the government’s rules and are therefore ineffectual, and then to a woman who breaks with the activists in order to transport three young men from Congo to a safe house.

Perhaps the most shocking scene in the film is the most familiar. We are suddenly on another border, the one between Poland and Ukraine, where white Eastern Europeans welcome other white Eastern Europeans with open arms. Holland has made a film about European racism today as the resurrection of its Nazi past, but I cannot imagine that audiences in the United States will watch Green Border without reflecting on the migration crisis at our own southern border.

The following interview is compiled and edited from two conversations with Holland, one in October 2023, the other in June 2024.

Green Border was released in Poland just a few weeks before the 2023 parliamentary election. The film had a serious effect. Specifically, the prime minister and the head of the then-ruling Law and Justice party took to social media to call it a collection of lies, shameful, and disgusting; and the minister of justice compared you to Josef Goebbels.

The response was different from what I expected. The attacks by the highest officials in government were unprecedented, even compared to Communist times. This aroused the curiosity of the general audience, especially those opposed to the [far-right] Law and Justice party government, so people went to the theaters in large numbers. And in the Q&As after the screenings, the response was more powerful than for any of my films before. The film played a part in mobilizing people, and influenced them to go out and vote against the ruling party. But unfortunately, the new democratic government has a lot of problems because the previous government—the authoritarian, nationalistic party—is still very influential and they’ve undermined many institutions, and we still have the same president. So now the new government has adopted the populist language of the so-called European mainstream. And 85 percent of the population is supporting this position. So you see how easy it is to spread this racist, nationalist hysteria. And when you have some aggression coming from the migrants, mostly orchestrated by political power plays, it triggers this moral hysteria, which goes beyond the facts. The result is that now the soldiers are allowed to shoot migrants, pretty much at will. The soldiers know they won’t be prosecuted. My worst fears are meeting reality. And I’m pessimistic about where it will go in the future.

Is this the case on all of Poland’s borders, even on the border with Ukraine?

No, you cannot shoot Ukrainians coming into Poland, or Black people who have been living in Ukraine.

The southern border here in the U.S. is also a site of chaos, much of it engineered by people who are trying to destabilize our democratic government by enticing people from Latin America to migrate, telling them that it’s easy to enter the U.S. And with the election coming up, the Republicans, having blocked the moderate bill that the Biden administration drew up, have forced Biden to take really terrible positions.

It is the same in Europe. The Democrats [the center-right Civic Coalition] in Poland are making the mistake that is already happening in Germany and France. The politicians have not learned a lesson, and neither have the people. The politicians think that if they take over the fascist agenda, more people will vote for them. But how can you support a politician who says one thing and six months later does the opposite? We are losing our belief in human rights, the thing that makes us special. And if we lose that, we have nothing to defend. I think we may need another inoculation of totalitarian violence to understand what we have lost and to start over.

It’s amazing that you could make Green Border in Poland. I know you didn’t ask for state funding. But where did you shoot?

The forest on the border where these things are actually happening is a primeval one, and it belongs to the state. We knew we couldn’t shoot a movie like this there. We didn’t want the government to know what we were doing. And in fact, that forest is too far from Warsaw—we didn’t have travel money to go back and forth. But we had seen documentary coverage of what was happening in that forest, and there is a forest near us that looks enough like it. It was a limited space, but good enough to reconstruct what was really happening. The forest is really important. It needed to be realistic, but also like the forest in a horror story—how it would be for the refugees who came thinking they would be in a paradise. We shot the entire film in 24 days. We knew we had to work fast. We had two units shooting simultaneously. I directed the scenes in the forest—the complicated scenes. And my colleagues [Kamila Tarabura and Katarzyna Warzecha] directed the more intimate scenes. It was quite experimental. I like collective work and I like my collaborators to get involved in the creative process. I’ve worked that way for years, especially with my daughter Kasia Adamik. She was working on her own film, so she arrived late and helped me with the scenes in the forest, especially with the children.

I didn’t do storyboards for those scenes. I wanted scenes of total chaos. Nothing that happens is deliberately planned. They are not scenes of war or of liberation. It is the expression of violence and chaos and despair. I’ve been working with this cinematographer [Tomasz Naumiuk] for a long time. He has the intelligence of a storyteller. Without him, the movie could not have happened in this way.

The first section of the movie is almost unbearable to watch. How did you decide how many times to show the refugees being pushed back and forth across the border?

The factual horror of the situation is in the repetition, but, because it is unbearable, we had to decide how many times [we could show it]. We had two big pushes from one side and one from the other. And then we began to get involved in different storylines. It was pretty much like this in the script, but we made some changes in the editing because not every storyline is interesting. My philosophy, when I am not working with a linear storyline, is to create different entrances into the story, to see it from different angles and characters. So the experience of the film is not the same for everyone. Some people are more interested in the refugees, some in the border guard and his story, and some in the activists.

The film is also a lesson in how to act in a crisis like this one. The group of aid workers are not effective, and it’s not until the psychoanalyst decides to risk arrest by transporting the migrants out of the exclusion zone that something positive happens.

When we were doing the research we saw that, when the state is failing, there are two ways you can go: you can look for solutions for the good of others on your own, or you can follow the state law, which isn’t working. In the fascist state during the Holocaust, everything was done as the state decreed. But when the state is an illegitimate, fascist state, you have to act on your own. So I’m old enough to say: fight the state.

But in relation to the border crisis here and in Europe, hardly anyone is doing anything.

No, except these small groups in Italy and France, and in Poland and Lithuania, but they are small, unrelated groups. I’m not so in touch with what is happening in the U.S., where everyone is so caught up by the fear of Trump or some other monster that it appears that they can’t act. But you have to act, because the monsters won’t disappear.

A lot of people here think Putin is great.

And a lot of people in Africa do as well. Because we’ve failed. Western democracy has been lazy.

The first film of yours that I saw, A Lonely Woman (1981), is the only film you’ve made that doesn’t have a glimmer of hope.

I don’t want people to go to the movies and feel hopeless and then sit in their room and drink vodka. Philosophically and existentially, I believe hope is necessary. And in Green Border , in that scene in the safe house, the kids of the rich Polish family who live there are rapping with the refugee kids from Congo. In spite of the problems with the internet, it can bring people together as never before. The kids from Congo, who have escaped because for them there is no future there, know the same music and video games as the Polish kids. Popular culture has become universal. These teenagers have something in common, so there is some kind of value in that—a value in entertainment.

At the end of the film, when you shift to the other border and see the Poles welcoming the Ukrainians, it no longer looks as positive as it did on CNN. It takes just about a half a second to realize that the entire migrant crisis is about racism.

I had thought for a while that the Holocaust inoculated us against racism, but it has come back and it’s visceral. It’s stronger than economic fear. The hate is visceral and it is coming back everywhere.

Very few other directors have the technical chops, the intelligence, and the sense of moral urgency to make a film like this. I think the speed at which you had to work translates into this sense of urgency. Did you learn about speed from working in television?

In television, you must work fast. What you learn is you don’t have to wait for the ideal. But anyway, I’m not a long thinker. I make decisions in the moment. I don’t feel that I lose my integrity when I’m working fast.

I’m curious about one decision you made. The very first image in the film—a drone shot above the forest—is in color and then the rest of the film is black and white. I thought that black and white makes the relationship to history very strong. But it’s also important to show the forest as it exists separate from the situation in the movie or the terrified subjectivity of the characters. I really want to know when you made that decision and why?

Technically, when you shoot digitally, you are always shooting in color. Then you have the choice to keep the color or take the color away. But this film always seemed stronger in black and white, so that wasn’t a difficult decision. But in the editing, when I watched that drone shot over the forest, I realized it was good to show the forest in color, but just once. You can make different interpretations of why it’s that way. That reality is black and white, or… I don’t know… It was just a spontaneous idea and it worked.

One last question. You just finished shooting a film about Kafka. Why do you want to make a film about him?

It is difficult to say why. It is rooted so deeply in an unconscious urge. Kafka was very important to me when I was 14 or 15. And after I read his letters, I saw this strange young man with neurotic double or triple identities and a visionary ability to look into the abyss, which touched me enormously. I felt, when I was young, that somehow he was my brother, and when I went to Prague to study, his presence became very powerful. In 1980, I adapted for television, with my then-husband [Laco Adamik], Kafka’s The Trial . It was shown recently because this is the hundredth anniversary of his death, and people have been writing to me about how relevant and strong that television film is. There are thousands of books written about him. His life is burdened now by those books and biographies. But when I was in Prague, his writings were almost forbidden, and then after the 1968 revolution, he became almost a tourist attraction. It’s all very paradoxical. We finished the shooting just last Sunday, so it’s very fresh. The structure is very fragmented, like a puzzle. There are elements coming from different directions, from his writing and from biographical elements, and even contemporary stuff. So I don’t have an idea of what will come out of it. It will be a big surprise to myself when I watch the first assembly. I’m terrified at this moment.

And who is the editor?

Pavel Hrdlička, the same editor I worked with on Green Border and Spoor and Charlatan (2020). He’s fearless and very sensitive, so I hope he’ll save it.

L’animation, Louis Clichy est tombé dedans quand il était petit. Comme tout le monde, vous nous direz, mais pour lui, cela représentait un peu plus que la distraction du matin au petit déjeuner. Influencé par une culture populaire et éclectique, qui va des Disney aux animés japonais, le réalisateur sait que son avenir se joue là : « Ça a toujours été un désir de carrière, mais effectivement, quand on est enfant, on s’imagine que c’est facile de faire ça. On comprend assez vite que ce n’est pas vrai. Mais l’idée même de faire de l’animation ne m’a jamais trop quitté. »

Entre les rêves de gosse et la réalité, le chemin exige toutefois un peu de persévérance. Il lui faudra « mettre beaucoup de temps à l’avoir » ce concours des Gobelins. Cinq ans en réalité, pendant lesquels il a végété un peu en fac d’histoire, avant d’atteindre ce graal. Déjà là se dessine le caractère de Louis Clichy, qui devient une évidence au moment où l’on commence à parler avec lui : une volonté farouche couplée à une capacité certaine à prendre son temps pour bien faire. À partir de cette école, pourtant, tout s’accélère. Un premier court métrage, Mange ! , exercice en 2D réalisé en deux semaines (en 2002), lui permet de trouver ce coup de crayon devenu signature : trait épais, dessin expressif, savant mélange d’efficacité et de cœur.

C’est en 2003, à la sortie de l’école, qu’il réalise le court qui change tout : À quoi ça sert l’amour ? , clip animé sur la chanson d’Édith Piaf, à la fois drôle, touchant, vivant, vibrant. Tellement qu’il tape dans l’œil de Pixar, qui l’embauche.

Animateur sur Wall-E ou Là-haut , il y apprend surtout une nouvelle gestion du travail : « J’aimais bien la manière de gérer cette boîte, évidemment avec beaucoup d’argent, ce qui facilite les choses. Cependant, il y a une manière assez saine d’investir et de responsabiliser tout le monde. »

Dans ce grand collectif, « tous les animateurs ont voix au chapitre, d’une manière assez horizontale, contrairement à la France où le réalisateur est omnipotent ». Des méthodes qu’il s’est employé à appliquer à son retour dans l’Hexagone quand on lui confie les rênes de deux Astérix ( Le Domaine des dieux, sorti en 2014,puis Le Secret de la Potion Magique, sorti en 2018),aux côtés d’Alexandre Astier. Réalisant au passage les deux plus gros succès récents de l’animation française, cumulant quelques 7 millions d’entrées. Impressionnant. Et déjà de quoi se satisfaire.

TROUVER SA VOIX

Cependant, pour Louis Clichy, la perspective d’un troisième volet a résonné comme une sonnette d’alarme. Le besoin, à 49 ans, de réaliser une œuvre qui soit sienne, de raconter quelque chose de proche : un « vrai » premier film, en somme.

Et cette histoire d’un jeune ado atteint de scoliose et grandissant dans le fin fond de la Beauce dans les années 1980 trottait déjà depuis un petit bout de temps dans sa tête : « À l’origine, c’était quelque chose de très ténu, mais je me suis dit que c’était mon moment. » Un récit qui a grandi pour devenir ce clin d’œil pudique à une enfance rurale, interrompue par le divorce de ses parents, qui l’a poussé vers la ville. Une déclaration d’amour aussi à cette adolescence mal-aimée : « C’est le moment des premiers émois, d’un corps qui devient lourd, rigide. C’est une contrainte imposée qu’on ne comprend qu’après coup. »

Une contrainte matérialisée par le corset qui donne son titre au film, et qu’il a lui-même porté : « Je voulais retrouver ce sentiment d’être engoncé comme dans une armure ». Objet d’exclusion, mais aussi artifice de création tant cet attirail oscille entre burlesque et héroïsme. Et quelle idée esthétique géniale que de voir ce gamin tordu au milieu de la rectitude parfaite des champs !

L’occasion aussi de renouer avec une technique qui lui ressemble. Après des années à manipuler les courbes lisses et parfaites de la 3D, Le Corset a permis à Louis Clichy de revenir à l’immédiateté du coup de crayon, à l’imperfection. Comme l’éclosion d’une identité explorée vingt-trois ans plus tôt : « J’ai voulu reprendre ce style-là parce que précisément, j’avais envie d’être dans quelque chose d’évanescent, un peu ‘‘carnet de croquis’’ ».

Un sentiment renforcé par l’aquarelle, qui donne l’impression que tout vient d’être jeté là, tout de suite, sur le papier. Comme une urgence. Celle de se retrouver et de nous permettre de le rencontrer, enfin. À quoi ça sert l’amour ? , demandait Édith Piaf. Celui de Louis Clichy pour l’animation nous permet de faire connaissance avec l’une des grandes voix du cinéma français.

: Le Corset de Louis Clichy (KMBO, 1h30), sortie le 14 octobre

article_text:
Am 1. November 2026 ist die Filmproduzentin Regina Ziegler im Alter von 82 Jahren verstorben. Die energische Frau mit den markanten roten Haaren zählte über fünf Jahrzehnte zu den einflussreichsten Produzentinnen der deutschen Film- und Fernsehbranche. Mit mehr als 500 Filmen fürs Kino und Fernsehen prägte sie die deutsche Filmgeschichte maßgeblich mit.

Regina Ziegler wurde 1944 in Quedlingburg geboren und gründete 1973 die nach ihr benannte Produktionsfirma Regina Ziegler Film . Zunächst studierte sie Jura, brach das Studium aber schon nach einem Semester ab und suchte nach ersten Erfahrungen beim Sender Freies Berlin und als Produktionsleiterin bei Rosa von Praunheim ihren Weg als eigenständige Produzentin. Mit einer Mischung aus Dickköpfigkeit, Chuzpe und viel kämpferischem Mut behauptete sie sich als Frau in einem harten Männer-Business, auch wenn sie dabei als „Minusmillionärin“ immer wieder auf wohlwollende Geldgeber und Kooperationspartner angewiesen war, wie sie in ihrer Autobiografie „ Geht nicht, gibt’s nicht “ freimütig bekannte.

Dass sich dieser Einsatz dennoch lohnte, zeigte sich schon bei ihrem ersten, gemeinsam mit ihrem damaligen Ehemann Wolf Gremm produzierten Film „ Ich dachte, ich wäre tot “ (1974), der auf Anhieb einen Bundesfilmpreis gewann und sich als Favorit der Filmkritiker erwies. Im Laufe ihrer Karriere produzierte Regina Ziegler viele preisgekrönte Filme: „ Malou “ (1981) von Jeanine Meerapfel gewann in Cannes den FIPRESCI-Preis der internationalen Filmkritik und „ Novembertage “ (1990) von Marcel Ophüls den Adolf-Grimme-Preis; der Kurzfilm „ Der flämische Meister “ (1993) von Susan Seidelman, der erste Teil der Kurzfilmreihe „ Erotic Tales “ (1994-2003), war sogar für den „Oscar“ nominiert.

Insgesamt umfasst die Liste ihrer Arbeit über 500 Filme fürs Kino wie fürs Fernsehen, darunter so herausragende Werke wie „ Rückkehr nach Montauk “ (2017) von Volker Schlöndorff, „ Henri 4 “ (2010) von Jo Baier, „ Solo für Klarinette “ (1998) von Nico Hoffmann, „ Korczak “ (1990) von Andrzej Wajda oder „ Fabian “ (1979) von Wolf Gremm. Zu ihren bekanntesten Werken zählen die Serie „ Weissensee “ (2010-1028) und die Musical-Verfilmung „ Ich war noch niemals in New York “ (2019).

Internationale Anerkennung fand Regina Ziegler unter anderem auch durch eine Retrospektive im Museum of Modern Art New York. 2016 wurde sie bei der Verleihung des Deutschen Filmpreises mit dem Ehrenpreis für herausragende Verdienste um den Deutschen Film ausgezeichnet. In der Laudatio hob Iris Berben insbesondere ihre „Leidenschaft, Energie, Charme, Durchsetzungskraft und eine unendlich große Liebe zu ihrem Metier“ hervor.

Ihr letztes großes Projekt war die Verfilmung „ Heimsuchung – Eine Jahrhundertgeschichte " (2026) durch Volker Schlöndorff nach dem gleichnamigen Roman von Jenny Erpenbeck. Der Film feierte seine Premiere bei den Filmfestspielen in Cannes und ist aktuell noch in den deutschen Kinos zu sehen.

Seit der Jahrtausendwende wird die Produktionsfirma Ziegler Film auch von Zieglers Tochter Tanja Ziegler als Mitgeschäftsführerin geleitet. Allen Verlockungen, unter das Dach eines finanzkräftigen Konzerns zu schlüpfen, hat die mittelständische Firma bislang widerstanden. Von diesem widerständigen Geist kündet auch das Engagement für das Berliner Traditionskino „ filmkunst 66 “, das Mutter und Tochter 2011 übernommen haben. Ihr „unermüdlicher Einsatz für den Film und ihr Mut werden uns immer in Erinnerung bleiben“, schrieb Tanja Ziegler in der Notiz, mit der sie den Tod ihrer Mutter am 1. November 2026 öffentlich machte.

article_text:
To mark the 50th anniversary of Tom Petty & The Heartbreakers , Morrison Hotel Gallery joins forces with the late-great artist’s estate to present Tom Petty: An American Dreamer .

Opening in West Hollywood this Thursday, October 15 (7:30–9:30PM) and in New York City next Thursday, October 22 (6–8PM), this photographic retrospective — featuring exclusive imagery and an ultra-limited edition of handwritten lyrics reproduced from the “Free Fallin’” virtuoso’s personal archive — spans Petty’s extraordinary career from the emergence of The Heartbreakers in the 1970s through his solo work, collaborations, and final years onstage.

More than a portrait of a musician, Tom Petty: An American Dreamer offers an intimate visual history of an American original: the songwriter, performer, rebel, romantic and enduring cultural icon whose music defined generations, on public view through 11/8.
